name: Mandelic acid

lead: Mandelic acid is an alpha-hydroxy acid used as a chemical exfoliant for acne, dark spots, uneven pigmentation and photoaging. It is sold in serums and professional peels and favoured by people with sensitive skin.

Its molecule is larger than glycolic acid's, which is said to slow penetration and reduce irritation, and as an AHA it promotes exfoliation and cell turnover, leaving fewer clogged pores and smoother, more even skin. A Cochrane review covered AHAs for acne as a class, and registered trials compare mandelic peels with tranexamic acid for melasma and test a combined peel around the eyes.

paras: It is used as a leave-on serum a few evenings a week or as a professional peel, and often built up slowly. Sunscreen is generally advised with AHA products, and results show over weeks.
Common AHA effects are stinging, redness and peeling, and sun sensitivity is a consideration. The sources give little mandelic-acid-specific safety data.

chain: Fewer clogged pores and dark spots
angle.text: Mandelic acid gently exfoliates dead cells, so pores clog less and dark spots fade for smoother, more even skin. Dedicated clinical evidence is limited, with most support coming from related AHAs.

lead: Mandelic acid (2-hydroxy-2-phenylacetic acid) is a chiral alpha-hydroxy acid with the formula C8H8O3 [1]. In cosmetics and dermatology it is used as a chemical exfoliant for acne, hyperpigmentation and photoaging [1].

An encyclopedic summary says it penetrates skin more slowly than smaller AHAs such as glycolic acid because of its larger molecule, and therefore causes less irritation, and cites formulation studies reporting acne lesion reductions of up to 69% [1]. That summary is AI-generated and its citations were not verified here.

Controlled clinical evidence specific to mandelic acid is sparse. A Cochrane review assessed topical alpha-hydroxy acids for acne as a group, and registered trials are examining mandelic peels in melasma and in a periocular peel [2][3][4].

paras: Cosmetic uses include chemical peels and serums for acne-prone, pigmented or photoaged skin, with exfoliation attributed to the acid's cell-turnover effect [1]. Mandelic acid is also studied as a natural preservative: a 2024 paper examined emulsions formulated with mandelic acid and essential oils as sustainable preservatives [5].

A 2020 Cochrane review of topical azelaic acid, salicylic acid, nicotinamide, sulphur, zinc and alpha-hydroxy acids for acne included 49 randomized trials with 3,880 participants and examined patient self-assessment, withdrawals, minor adverse events and quality of life; mandelic acid was not the review's sole subject [2]. A 2022 network meta-analysis of acne treatments covers other topical and oral options [6].

A registered trial of 120 participants (not yet recruiting) plans to compare intralesional tranexamic acid with a mandelic acid peel for melasma [3]. A completed phase IV registration of 12 participants evaluated a 'duosomal' chemical peel for aesthetic enhancement of periocular and facial regions [4]. A randomized trial of a peel formulated with polyhydroxy acids across skin types, including sensitive skin, is a different acid class [7]. No large randomized trial of mandelic acid alone for acne or pigmentation is available in the published literature.
Encyclopedic summaries describe mandelic acid as gentler than smaller AHAs [1]. The published literature contain no mandelic acid-specific safety trial.

A 2005 T Nation thread on fighting acne includes one user's report that a mandelic acid lotion helped their acne [8]. This is an individual anecdote; looksmaxxing forums are not otherwise documented to discuss it in the available sources.
